'''Burduna''' (Purduna) is an [[Australian Aboriginal languages|Aboriginal language]] that was traditionally spoken in the region between the [[Ashburton River (Western Australia)|Ashburton]] and [[Gascoyne River]]s in the [[Pilbara]] region of [[Western Australia]]. It belongs to the [[Kanyara languages|Kanyara]] group of languages, which also includes [[Pinikura language|Binigura/Pinikura]], [[Thalanyji language|Thalanyji]], and [[Bayungu language|Bayungu]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Austin|first=Peter|date=1988|title=Classification of southern Pilbara languages|journal=Papers in Australian Linguistics|volume=17|pages=1–17}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Dixon|first=Robert M.|title=Australian languages: their nature and development|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2002|isbn=9780521473781|language=English}}</ref>

The language is currently classified as critically endangered, with no recorded native speakers by 1994.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=Burduna|url=https://www.wangkamaya.org.au/pilbara-languages/burduna |access-date=2026-04-16 |website=Wangka Maya Pilbara Aboriginal Language Centre }}</ref> However, there are some people of Burduna heritage who can still speak and recognise a few words and phrases.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=W24: Burduna {{!}} aiatsis collection|url=https://collection.aiatsis.gov.au/austlang/language/w24|url-status=live|access-date=December 17, 2021|website=collection.aiatsis.gov.au|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181031164345/https://collection.aiatsis.gov.au/austlang/language/w24 |archive-date=31 October 2018 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Austin|first=Peter|date=1988|title=Aboriginal languages of the Gascoyne-Ashburton region|url=http://www.peterkaustin.com/docs/LTUWP_ga_2020-09-01.pdf|journal=La Trobe Working Papers in Linguistics|volume=1|pages=43–63|via=La Trobe University}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=Purduna|url=https://www.sorosoro.org/en/purduna/|url-status=live|access-date=December 17, 2021|website=Sorosoro|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110105175315/http://www.sorosoro.org/en/purduna |archive-date=5 January 2011 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Burgman |first=Albert |title=Burduna dictionary : English-Burduna wordlist and thematic wordlist 2007 |publisher=South Hedland, WA : Wangka Maya Pilbara Aboriginal Language Centre |year=2007}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Burgman |first=Albert |title=Bayungu dictionary : English-Bayungu wordlist and thematic wordlist 2007 |publisher=Wangka Maya Pilbara Language Centre |year=2007}}</ref>

== History ==

=== Evolution ===
Burduna has been classified as a [[double-marking language]]. Although it has been categorised as a Kanyara language, it is significantly different from the other languages in the category as it underwent a number of changes in pronunciation.<ref name=":3" />

Over the years, the language lost most of its nasal sounds and tones. Certain words that contains peripheral stops with ''p''  and ''k'' sounds [[Lenition|lenited]] to a ''w'' sound instead. For example, ''papu'' 'father' became ''{{lang|bxn|pawu}}'', and ''puka'' 'bad' became ''{{lang|bxn|puwa}}.'' However, this lenition did not occur when the previous syllable contained a ''w''. Instead, the consonants ''p'' and ''k'' descended, and were pronounced as ''b'' and ''g'' respectively.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last=Austin |first=Peter |date=1981 |title=Proto-Kanyara and proto-Mantharta historical phonology |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0024384181900097 |journal=Lingua |language=en |volume=54 |issue=4 |pages=295–333 |doi=10.1016/0024-3841(81)90009-7|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Another marked difference included the pronunciation of polysyllabic words such as ''{{lang|bxn|yakan}}'' 'spouse' and ''{{lang|bxn|pukurra}}'' 'devil'. These words lost their middle consonants and were shortened to ''yaan'' and ''puurra.'' The vowels were pronounced with a long, drawn-out sound.<ref name=":4" />

Burduna words also contained consonant clusters in words such as ''gb'' in ''dagba'' 'spider' or ''rdg'' in ''{{lang|bxn|ngardga}}'' 'beard'. Furthermore, words that originally contained consonant clusters underwent lenition and were pronounced with softer sounds. For example, ''mb'' was pronounced as ''p'', ''nd'' as ''t'', and ''ngg'' as ''k''.<ref name=":4" />

In addition, where other languages have a ''dh'' or a ''j'' in the middle of words, Burduna evolved to contain a ''y.'' For example, the Thalanyji word ''{{lang|dhl|ngadhal}}'' 'cousin' has its Burduna complement spelt as ''{{lang|bxn|ngayal}}.''<ref name=":4" />

=== Extinction ===
As a result of white settlement along the Ashburton and Gascyone river regions, the language ceased to be used, and is believed to have died out sometime during the first half of the twentieth century. There are a few people living in Onslow and Carnarvon who can still speak and recognize a few words and phrases, but the majority of Burduna descendants have intermarried with other language groups. The ''National Language Indigenous 2004 Survey'' estimated that there are no native speakers of the language. It has thus been classified as endangerment level 0.<ref name=":2" />

==Culture and development==
The [[Burduna people]] were located around the Nyang and Maroonah regions between the Ashburton and Gascyone rivers in north-western Australia. Their traditional country regions included the regions around the Yannarie and Lyndon rivers. Some of the area in and around the Towera region is also identified as being traditional Burduna land.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Austin|first=Peter|date=1988|title=Classification of southern Pilbara languages|journal=Papers in Australian Linguistics|volume=17|pages=1–17}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=W24: Burduna {{!}} aiatsis collection|url=https://collection.aiatsis.gov.au/austlang/language/w24|url-status=live|access-date=December 17, 2021|website=collection.aiatsis.gov.au|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181031164345/https://collection.aiatsis.gov.au/austlang/language/w24 |archive-date=31 October 2018 }}</ref>

The [[Kanyara languages|Kanyara]] people traditionally spoke three different languages - Purduna or Burduna, Thalanyji, and [[Bayungu language|Bayungu]] or Payungu. The three languages share highly similar sentence structure and vocabulary, with 60-70% of words being common across all three of them.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Austin|first=Peter|date=1991|title=Double case marking in Kanyara and Mantharta languages, Western Australia|url=http://www.peterkaustin.com/docs/LTUWP_doublecase_2020-09-01.pdf|journal=La Trobe Working Papers in Linguistics|volume=4|pages=19–36|via=La Trobe University}}</ref>
== Grammar ==

=== Word classes ===
There are two major word classes and three minor ones in the Burduna language. The first major word class contains the [[Nominal (linguistics)|nominal words]], which includes [[noun]]s and [[adjective]]s, names, [[pronoun]]s, [[demonstrative]]s, and [[cardinal direction]]s.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Austin|first=Peter|date=1991|title=Double case marking in Kanyara and Mantharta languages, Western Australia|url=http://www.peterkaustin.com/docs/LTUWP_doublecase_2020-09-01.pdf|journal=La Trobe Working Papers in Linguistics|volume=4|pages=19–36|via=La Trobe University}}</ref>

The second major word group includes the [[verb]]s. The three minor word groups include [[adverb]]s, [[Grammatical particle|particles]], and [[interjection]]s.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Austin|first=Peter|date=1991|title=Double case marking in Kanyara and Mantharta languages, Western Australia|url=http://www.peterkaustin.com/docs/LTUWP_doublecase_2020-09-01.pdf|journal=La Trobe Working Papers in Linguistics|volume=4|pages=19–36|via=La Trobe University}}</ref>
